report.hypothesisVerdict: Partly right: the script side was Bash, but the reason was Claude Code's permission system. The path was fixed in eb8f0f44 (27 May, "migrate agent personas to agentskills.io format"), and docs/agent-skills.md:14-44 records why. Allowlist rules compare literal command text. A `$VAR` in a command the model types always prompts ("simple_expansion", GH#51001). A subagent's working folder may be a sub-repo, so skill text spelt the full ~/git/defra/... path, and the scripts copied it as $HOME/git/defra/... "for consistency" (agent-skills.md:29-32). Bash never needed it: scripts/stack/run-stack.sh:4-5 finds its root from its own location. Later commits locked it in. 564e594b added the `make link` symlink. fcbadde9 denied `bash *`/`node *` and collapsed the allowlist onto the literal tools/** path. 7578ee29 made the canonical path a real clone. 4918fba0 gave tim a last-resort fallback to it. Moving the scripts into tim does remove the script half: `Bash(tim:*)` (.claude/settings.json:87) has no path, and tim walks up from the current folder (tim/src/env/workspace-root.js:57-85). It also reads the same JIRA_*/SONAR_TOKEN variables, so nobody changes their setup. But the path stays fixed unless the plan also rewrites the model-typed layer: 18 allowlist lines (settings.json:63-93), about 1,000 mentions in 114 skill files plus 7 rules files, the workflow scripts (increment-build-loop.js:407, designer-prototyping-suite.js:45) and the 8 repo hook lines.

realBlockers.name: Stack ownership not enforced across clones (shared compose project name, stack commands that ignore the lease, lease ignores workspace)
realBlockers.why: Every clone drives the one `trade-imports` project (docker/stack/compose.yml:1). A plain `tim docker dev` writes no lease, and tim docker up/dev/down only refuse when a lease exists (tim/src/commands/docker/index.js:52-56). So clone B's up rebuilds clone A's containers from B's repos/ (dev.compose.yml ../../repos), and B's down runs `down --volumes` on A's data (stop-stack.sh:42). The lease records `workspace` (stack-lease.js:319) but nothing compares it, and the fixed holder 'perf' (lease.js:215) can be reused or released from another clone.
realBlockers.fix: Keep the single project name. Refuse when the running containers' com.docker.compose.project.working_dir label, or lease.workspace, is another clone, with --force to override. Also compare workspace in acquire and release.

realBlockers.name: tools/ bash scripts hardcode the canonical path (journey-builder worktrees and branches included)
realBlockers.why: About 130 tools scripts set WORKSPACE=$HOME/git/defra/trade-imports-workspace (for example prepare-digest.sh:16, style-add-item.sh:75, start-service-tag.sh:34). Run from clone 2, they read and write clone 1's workareas/ and repos/. journey-builder makes worktrees and spike/ and spec/ branches in clone 1 (prepare-digest.sh:52-54, :75-77).
realBlockers.fix: Find the root from BASH_SOURCE (with TIM_WORKSPACE as an override) right away, then port each folder to tim, which walks up from the current folder.
realBlockers.fixedBy: P02, P03 (then the per-folder ports; P63 retires journey-builder)

realBlockers.name: Globally linked tim runs one clone's code
realBlockers.why: `which tim` resolves through npm link to ~/git/defra/trade-imports-workspace/tim/src/cli.js, so clone 2 runs clone 1's tim code, node_modules and branch. Its auto-pull updates clone 2, but the code that runs is still clone 1's.
realBlockers.fix: The global tim becomes a launcher that hands over to the nearest clone's own tim/src/cli.js.

realBlockers.name: repos.json roster read from beside tim's code
realBlockers.why: tim/src/constants/repos.js:16-22,71 loads the first repos.json found (the one beside tim's code) once at module load, before --workspace is parsed, so clone 2 acts on its own folders with clone 1's repo list.
realBlockers.fix: Load the roster lazily from the resolved workspace root.

realBlockers.name: Build loop and prototype workflows resolve a fixed workspace
realBlockers.why: increment-build-loop.js:407-411 takes the first of three fixed candidates (clone 1 always wins) and has no override, so a loop launched from clone 2 builds, commits, takes the lease and runs `codex exec -C` in clone 1 (:3106). prepare-handoff.js:94, port-kit-page.js:77 and designer-prototyping-suite.js:44-45 (a literal /Users/samfarrington path) are fixed too.
realBlockers.fix: config.workspace as distil.js already does, otherwise resolve from the session folder or CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR.

realBlockers.name: Permission allowlist tied to the canonical path
realBlockers.why: 18 entries (.claude/settings.json:63-93) name ~/git/defra/trade-imports-workspace, so clone 2's own tools/ and repos/ commands prompt, while commands aimed at clone 1 are auto-allowed. The prefix rule at :84 also matches ...-workspace-2. Together with the skill text, this steers agents into clone 1.
realBlockers.fix: Prove which relative patterns match (with Sam watching), move script calls to Bash(tim:*), drop the canonical entries, and rewrite the skill text.

realBlockers.name: Local E2E from a clone that does not own the stack
realBlockers.why: The tests repo hard-codes localhost frontends (playwright.docker-compose.config.ts:10-13) and defaults the backend and Mongo URLs to localhost (:19-27). An E2E run from clone 2 silently tests clone 1's code and data, and nothing checks ownership.
realBlockers.fix: A Playwright globalSetup and the tim gate refuse unless this clone owns the stack (lease workspace or container label); ALLOW_FOREIGN_STACK=1 is the escape hatch.

realBlockers.name: Fit-test host ports 3050/3052/3053
realBlockers.why: Each frontend's test:fit:ci hard-codes PORT inline (package.json), and gates.json fixes the same ports. Two clones running the same frontend's fit rung at once: one is refused (gate.js:212-234). The rung needs no stack, so clones without one hit this.
realBlockers.fix: Use `PORT=${PORT:-N}` in each frontend, and have the gate move to the next free port.

realBlockers.name: Lease logs shared by every clone (minor)
realBlockers.why: logsDirFor defaults to ~/.local/state/tim/logs (lease.js:62-63) and runToLog truncates the file on each run (exec.js:84-88), so the last acquire or release from any clone replaces the previous log. Debug history only.

realBlockers.name: Plants prototype port 3103 (minor, run-time)
realBlockers.why: Two prototypes at once clash on 3103. The sign-in redirects, the session cookie and the Redis prefix also default to the same values (config.js:58-62, 224-235, 270-272, 302-306).
realBlockers.fix: Run the second one with PORT, DEFRA_ID_REDIRECT_URL, DEFRA_ID_SIGN_OUT_REDIRECT_URL, AUTH_SESSION_COOKIE_NAME and REDIS_KEY_PREFIX set. The Defra ID stub accepts any redirect URI, so it needs no change.

sharpEdges: Each extra clone needs its own `tim workspace setup` (a full repos/), `npm ci` inside tim/, and a copy of the gitignored config/machine.json (or TIM_MACHINE_CONFIG).
Two clones pushing the same branch name race at the remote. Keep one branch per clone; the same-name rule across repos still holds within a clone.

tim run from outside any clone (home folder, scratchpad, a workflow agent's folder) falls back to the canonical clone. Workflow briefs should pass --workspace or set TIM_WORKSPACE. P69 adds a warning.

Several ports change behaviour on purpose. theme-ticket push becomes a dry run until --confirm (P36 must add --confirm to SKILL.md:330 in the same commit). JSON output moves into tim's envelope, so skill jq paths read .result. The push check finds the PR from SonarCloud, so a brand-new PR's first push gets branch scope.

Rule 8 moves GitHub calls out of scripts into skill text (gh search prs, gh pr view, gh pr diff in review, style and understanding-check). A subagent that skips a gh step leaves a repo out; the tim side must refuse loudly when the fact files are missing.
Hooks that call node must fail closed safely: guard on tim/node_modules existing. The guard hooks stay Bash for exactly this reason (P19).
Relative Bash allowlist patterns are untested: P11 must be run with Sam watching, because a session cannot see its own prompts.
Each repo-rooted Claude session starts a sonar MCP container of about 0.5-0.8 GiB. More clones open at once means more memory, but no collision.

Claude project memory and transcripts are keyed by absolute path, so clone 2 gets a fresh project (auto memory is off anyway). ~/.codex/config.toml trusts paths, and the build loop already bypasses that.
Sam's user-level ~/.claude/settings.json:192-198 auto-mode notes name only the canonical path. P71 updates them.
Retiring journey-builder (P63) is a scope call, not a port. The fallback port rows exist in the folder plan if Sam wants to keep it.
govuk-upgrade's changelog fetch from raw.githubusercontent.com moves into a tim client. I read that as a static file fetch, not the GitHub API, so rule 8 does not forbid it.
report.ciOnlyColleague: A colleague who never runs the stack needs only the path fixes, not the stack work. Once P01-P05 land, their clone can sit anywhere, run its own tim, and keep its own workareas/, branches and build-loop runs. They never take the stack lease, so P06 never refuses them. P07 stops them running local E2E against someone else's stack by accident. E2E comes from GitHub Actions: each service repo's PR calls the reusable e2e-tests.yml, which runs the suites and tags for that repo listed in config/e2e-tests-pr-scope.json. That is the evidence on their PR, and the build loop already waits on PR checks (wait-for-pr-checks.sh). The fit rungs and unit tests run natively with no stack. P08 lets their fit ports move if another clone on the same machine holds them. The one gap today: tim build gate's E2E rung needs the local stack, so a CI-only clone cannot pass the loop's gate. P10 adds an opt-in `--e2e ci` mode that leaves that rung to the PR's e2e check. What they lose: CI E2E follows the PR scope file, which can run less than the local gate, and each attempt waits a CI cycle. Their setup does not change otherwise: the same JIRA_USER, JIRA_TOKEN, JIRA_BASE_URL and SONAR_TOKEN in ~/.zshrc, and gh's own login.
report.inFlight: The remove-makefile branch (chore/NO_JIRA-remove-makefile) is now committed: 7 commits ahead of origin/main (9fa9d027 to 9f3b62a9). Only dockws/ is untracked. The inventory's "uncommitted" note is out of date. The branch is the first slice of this plan (Make into tim). It adds `tim start` for every service, `tim docker logs`, --help on the stack scripts with help.test.sh, and drops the Makefile marker from workspace-root.js. This plan should start from that branch once it merges, not from main. P12 (delete scripts/setup.sh and update.sh, whose only caller was the Makefile) and P58 (which builds on help.test.sh and logs.js) depend on it. It does not touch the path coupling: scripts/stack already finds its root from its own location. One loose end it leaves: the Makefile's docker-local-branches target (origin/main Makefile:182) has no tim replacement. Port it or retire it deliberately before merging. dockws/ is not a second workspace. It holds 3 files dated 2 Nov: a Makefile containing 'all:', a run-stack.sh that just does 'exit 0', and an empty repos/. That matches the old tim test fixtures exactly, so a test leaked it into the current folder. It is safe to delete and unrelated to this plan. workareas/shared/parallel-alt-stacks/plan.md (31 Aug, never built) wanted several stacks with port blocks, and "scripts stay the source of truth". This plan supersedes it: one stack per machine, CI for E2E, and Bash moved into tim.

path-census.originReason:
The path was hardcoded on 27 May 2026 in eb8f0f44, "chore(EUDPA-179): migrate agent personas to agentskills.io format". It is a squash of 122 commits. Its body says "Register skills + permission allowlist in .claude/settings.json; hardcode canonical workspace path". The same commit wrote the rationale that is still in docs/agent-skills.md:14-44.

1. Claude Code's permission check flags any `$VAR` in a command the model types as "Contains simple_expansion", even when that variable is allowlisted (GH#51001, cited at docs/agent-skills.md:34-39 and :85-88). So a command like `$WS/tools/x.sh` always prompts.
2. Allowlist rules compare literal strings. `~/git/...` and `/Users/<you>/git/...` count as different prefixes (agent-skills.md:89-92), and a relative `tools/x.sh` is listed as an anti-pattern (agent-skills.md:175).
3. Skills and spawned subagents cannot rely on the current directory. Inside `repos/<svc>`, `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` returns the sub-repo, not the workspace (agent-skills.md:16-21). Spawn prompts therefore name absolute `references/` paths (agent-skills.md:237).
4. An earlier walk-up helper using `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}` or `$PWD` broke in two ways: off-by-one errors when scripts moved depth, and false matches on a stray parent `.claude/` (agent-skills.md:41-44).

The two-layer convention follows from this. Commands the model types use the literal `~/git/defra/...` path, so the committed allowlist matches them. Scripts then copied that path as `$HOME/git/defra/...` for consistency (agent-skills.md:29-32), not because bash needed it.

How it evolved:
- 2cfa6e68 (8 April): the first commit already wrote `~/git/defra/trade-imports-animals/...` into persona prose.
- 564e594b (27 May): added `make link` to symlink the canonical path, "required by tools/".
- fcbadde9 (9 June): curated the allowlist. It added deny rules for `bash *`, `node *`, `python *` and others, and collapsed the per-domain entries into `~/git/defra/trade-imports-workspace/tools/**`. Scripts can therefore only be run by literal path, never as `bash tools/x.sh`.
- 4918fba0 (7 August): gave tim a fallback to the canonical path. tim already walked up from the current directory, "so worktrees and second clones keep resolving to themselves".
- f63153e0 and e277e6d9 (18 August): renamed `trade-imports-animals-workspace` to `trade-imports-workspace`.
- 7578ee29 (18 August): made the canonical path a clone, not a symlink. The symlink rule "existed because the repo name and the canonical name disagreed". `tim link` stayed as an escape hatch.

docs/agent-onboarding.md:28-31 now states the constraint as "every LLM-typed Bash command, every helper script, and the .claude/settings.json allowlist patterns hardcode that path".
path-census.bashHypothesis:
Partly right. The cause was Claude Code's permission system, not bash.

Bash does not need the literal path. Scripts can resolve their own location at runtime, and many already do:
- scripts/stack/run-stack.sh:4-5 uses BASH_SOURCE and needs no fixed path.
- About 64 tools/, scripts/ and hook files already resolve the workspace at runtime.
- 130 of the 186 tools/*.sh scripts copy `$HOME/git/defra/trade-imports-workspace` by convention, not because the shell requires it.

The real constraint is the model-typed layer:
- The allowlist has 18 literal-path entries (.claude/settings.json:63-93).
- The deny list blocks `bash *` and `node *` (settings.json:5-14), so scripts must be run by an absolute path that matches the allowlist.
- `$VAR` in a typed command trips simple_expansion.
- Skill text and spawn prompts need an absolute path, because the agent's current directory may be a sub-repo.

Moving scripts into tim does remove most of this. `Bash(tim:*)` at settings.json:87 is already path-free, and tim already finds the right clone by walking up from the current directory (tim/src/env/workspace-root.js:57-85). tim reads the same JIRA_* environment variables as the bash tools (tim/CLAUDE.md).

What tim does not fix, because these commands are model-typed rather than script calls:
- `git -C ~/...`, `npm --prefix ~/...`, `mvn -f ~/...`, `find`/`awk`/`sed ~/...` (settings.json:79-86).
- About 991 path mentions across 107 skill .md files and 22 in 7 rules files.

These need either current-directory-relative patterns such as `Bash(git -C repos/*:*)` plus agents that stay at the clone root, or a per-clone settings.local.json.

What I could and could not establish about relative allowlist patterns:
- Could establish: the repo's own committed evidence says relative forms prompt (agent-skills.md:175) and treats the rules as literal string compares (agent-skills.md:89-92). The guard-bash.sh hook already resolves relative executables against $CWD (guard-bash.sh:65-70), so hooks are not the blocker.
- Not tested: whether `Bash(./tools/**)` or `Bash(tools/**)` match. The task was read-only, and a session cannot see its own permission prompts (agent-skills.md:164-168).
- Not verified (offline, from Claude Code's documentation): Bash rules are prefix or glob matches on the raw command text, with no tilde, `$VAR` or relative-path resolution. Only Read/Edit rules have path anchoring (`//abs`, `~/`, `/` relative to the settings file, `./` relative to the current directory).

So a relative Bash pattern would probably match only when typed exactly that way, and only work when the current directory is the clone root.

The GH#51001 behaviour is cited in the repo but I did not re-test it.

sharedResources.evidence: docker/stack/compose.yml:1 (`name: trade-imports`). No -p or COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME is set in scripts/stack/lib/compose.sh:6-15 or run-stack.sh:351. tim hardcodes the same name in tim/src/exec/stack.js:86 (STACK_PROJECT) and filters on it at stack.js:150. tim/src/build/ports.js:54 uses it too.
sharedResources.collidesWhenTwoClonesExist: Not while only one clone runs the stack. This is the single-stack invariant the lease relies on: every clone addresses the same project. The hazard is that any clone can act on the stack another clone started. `docker compose up` from clone B with the same project name recreates clone A's containers from B's compose files and B's repos/. A `down` from B tears A's stack down (stop-stack.sh:42, `down --volumes --remove-orphans`). If the project name were made per-clone, tim's lease and port detection (stack.js:86/150, ports.js:54) would stop seeing the other clone's stack. So it must stay one machine-global name.

sharedResources.evidence: tim/src/exec/stack-lease.js:44-58 (defaultLeasePath: TIM_STACK_LEASE, else $XDG_STATE_HOME or ~/.local/state, then tim/stack-lease.json, 'one file per machine'). Lock at stack-lease.js:211-233 (mkdir is atomic). The lease records the starting clone at stack-lease.js:319 (`workspace: workspaceRoot`). tim docker lease --help says the same (commands/docker/lease.js:233).
sharedResources.collidesWhenTwoClonesExist: No. It is machine-wide, which is what 'only one runs the stack' needs. Gaps: (1) acquire and reuse compare only `holder`, never `lease.workspace` (stack-lease.js:142, 538, 564). A holder name both clones share, such as `tim docker perf`'s default holder 'perf' (lease.js:215), lets clone B reuse or release clone A's stack. Build-run holders are timestamped run ids, so in practice they are unique. (2) Setting TIM_STACK_LEASE differently per clone would break the guarantee.

sharedResources.scope: machine-global (they act on the one project)
sharedResources.evidence: tim/src/commands/docker/index.js:52-56 refuses only when a lease file exists. A stack started with plain `tim docker dev` writes no lease. The scripts themselves never read the lease: run-stack.sh, stop-stack.sh:42, bounce-backend.sh:46, dev-service.sh:58-71.
sharedResources.collidesWhenTwoClonesExist: Yes. This is the real collision. Clone A runs `tim docker dev`, which takes no lease. Clone B then runs `tim docker dev` or `up`, which goes ahead and silently recreates A's containers from B's source. B's `tim docker down` wipes A's databases. bounce-backend.sh and `dev-service.sh rebuild` from B rebuild A's running backend from B's repos/. The same can happen today with one clone and a hand-started stack. It is more likely with several clones. Fix: make every stack-starting and stack-stopping command take or check the lease, and record and compare `workspace`.

stack-state.leaseMechanism:
The lease is per machine, so it already fits "only one clone runs the stack at a time".

How it works:
- The lease is one JSON file at TIM_STACK_LEASE, otherwise $XDG_STATE_HOME/tim/stack-lease.json, otherwise ~/.local/state/tim/stack-lease.json (tim/src/exec/stack-lease.js:44-58).
- Writes are guarded by an atomic mkdir lock at `<lease>.lock`, which is broken when stale (stack-lease.js:211-272).
- The file records holder, mode, `workspace` (the absolute root of the clone that started the stack, stack-lease.js:319), the branches of its repos, pid, container ids and source fingerprints.
- Liveness is checked through `docker ps --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=trade-imports` (tim/src/exec/stack.js:86, 145-158). That works because every clone uses the same compose project name (docker/stack/compose.yml:1).
- Acquire starts a stack that is down, reuses a stack its holder already holds and refuses everything else (acquireDecision, stack-lease.js:136-148). Release runs the releasing clone's stop-stack.sh.

Gaps to close before several clones are safe:
1. The lease is opt-in. `tim docker up/dev/down/restart/bounce-backend` only refuse when a lease already exists (tim/src/commands/docker/index.js:52-56), and a plain `tim docker dev` takes none. scripts/stack/*.sh never read the lease. So clone B can recreate (`up`/`dev`) or wipe (`down --volumes`) a stack clone A started by hand. Fix: every start goes through the lease, and stop or rebuild is refused unless the caller's root matches `lease.workspace`.
2. Holder matching ignores `workspace` (stack-lease.js:142, 478, 538, 564). The fixed default holder 'perf' (commands/docker/lease.js:215) could be reused or released across clones. Fix: compare `lease.workspace` as well.
3. Images built by --dev are tagged machine-wide as `trade-imports-trade-imports-<service>:latest` (dev.compose.yml `image: ''`). A recreate without --build can run another clone's image (bounce-backend.sh:46, dev-service.sh `restart`). Fix: always build, or tag per clone.
4. The project name must stay machine-global. A per-clone project name would hide one clone's stack from another clone's lease and port checks.

Every path in the stack and the lease is relative to the clone or to XDG; none hard-codes ~/git/defra/trade-imports-workspace. The scripts work out WORKSPACE_ROOT from their own location (run-stack.sh:5, stop-stack.sh:5, dev-service.sh:17, bounce-backend.sh:5), and .staged/ and the bind mounts resolve against the clone. So nothing in the Docker stack needs the canonical path. The constraint is "one stack per machine", and the lease covers it once gaps 1 and 2 are closed.

E2E: the tests repo hard-codes the localhost frontend ports (repos/trade-imports-ins-tests/playwright.docker-compose.config.ts:10-13). Local E2E from any clone therefore hits whichever stack is up. Only the clone named in lease.workspace should run local E2E; the other clones use GitHub Actions.

tokens.timContract:
tim reads the same environment variables directly, again with no .env or profile loading. The contract is in tim/README.md:1074-1085, which says tim "reuses the same environment variables as the bash tooling ... seamless pickup with no new setup".

| Variable | tim reader (path:line) | Same as Bash? |
|---|---|---|
| JIRA_USER, JIRA_TOKEN, JIRA_BASE_URL | tim/src/clients/jira-client.js:122-138; tim/src/clients/confluence-client.js:35-51 (adds `/wiki` like Bash); probed by `tim auth` (tim/src/commands/auth.js:15-41) through `/rest/api/2/myself` (jira-client.js:332, the endpoint tools/jira/auth.sh:21 uses) | Yes, same names and Basic auth. tim also trims a trailing slash from the base URL (jira-client.js:138, confluence-client.js:51), so it is slightly more lenient. Missing values raise AUTH or USAGE errors instead of `:?` exits. |
| JIRA_PROJECT_KEY | tim/src/commands/jira/epics.js:24, tim/src/commands/jira/search.js:54 (fallback when `--project` is not given) | Yes for epics and search. `tim jira create` takes the project from the tim-ticket/1 manifest (tim/src/commands/jira/manifest.js:18), not the env as tools/jira/create-ticket.sh:184 does. |
| Jira board id | tim/src/commands/build/start.js:40 (`--board`, default 13780) | Same default as tools/ticket-creator/prepare-ticket-creation.sh:19. No `tim jira` command moves a ticket to a board; only `tim build start` uses `moveToBoard` (tim/src/build/start.js:250). |
| SONAR_TOKEN | tim/src/clients/sonar-client.js:76 (optional Bearer token for `tim sonar gate` and `tim sonar issues`) | Same name. There is no zsh-profile fallback like scripts/sonar/sonar-push-gate.sh:97-100. |
| GitHub | none. Rule 8 (CLAUDE.md) and tim/README.md:976-985 keep GitHub on `gh`. `tim auth` checks Jira and Confluence only (auth.js:80). Clones use `https://github.com/${manifest.githubOrg}` (tim/src/constants/repos.js:154,162). | The clone URL and org come from the same repos.json as scripts/setup.sh:14,56. git credentials come from the user's git/gh credential helper in both. TIM_GITHUB_BASE_URL is a test-only override. |
| Workspace root | tim/src/env/workspace-root.js:57-87: `--workspace`, then TIM_WORKSPACE, then a walk up from the current directory, then the canonical path. Also the repos.json candidates (tim/src/constants/repos.js:17-22). | Not the same: tim finds whichever clone you stand in, while the Bash tools/ always use the canonical $HOME path. On this branch the Makefile marker was dropped from the walk-up (git diff origin/main -- tim/src/env/workspace-root.js). |
| Stack knobs | `tim docker` runs scripts/stack/*.sh through execa (tim/src/exec/exec.js:36,61,98), which passes the environment through by default, so STUB_PROFILE, DEV_BUILD_PLATFORM, the TRADE_IMPORTS_* tags, ZAP_* and the rest reach the scripts. tim checks STUB_PROFILE itself for `tim docker perf` (tim/src/exec/stack-lease.js:28-38, tim/src/commands/docker/lease.js:50-57). | Yes, while the scripts stay the implementation. A native rewrite has to re-read each one. |
| tim-only settings | TIM_NO_AUTO_PULL (tim/src/exec/auto-pull.js:45); TIM_STACK_LEASE and XDG_STATE_HOME (tim/src/exec/stack-lease.js:46-55, one lease file per machine); TIM_MACHINE_CONFIG (tim/src/build/machine-config.js:36, default `<workspace>/config/machine.json`); TIM_DOCKER_START_WAIT_MS and TIM_DOCKER_START_POLL_MS (tim/src/exec/docker-daemon.js:25-26); CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR (tim/src/build/runs/archive.js:45, tim/src/commands/backlog/index.js:531) | New and optional, all with defaults. No user setup is needed. |
gaps: The credentials already match: JIRA_USER, JIRA_TOKEN and JIRA_BASE_URL are read under the same names, with the same Basic auth, the same /wiki suffix for Confluence and the same /rest/api/2/myself probe. Moving Jira and Confluence scripts into tim needs no change to anyone's setup.

SONAR_TOKEN has no profile fallback in tim. scripts/sonar/sonar-push-gate.sh:97-100 reads it from `zsh -ic 'printenv SONAR_TOKEN'` when the hook runs without it (a Claude app launched from the Dock). tim/src/clients/sonar-client.js:76 reads only the process environment. A tim port of the pre-push gate has to keep that fallback, or keep the hook in bash.

The Jira and Confluence variables have no profile fallback either, in Bash or in tim. Both rely on the calling shell having exported them. That is no regression, but a tim command run from a hook launched outside a shell would see them missing, just as Bash would.

Workspace root: the Bash tools/ scripts write in WORKSPACE="$HOME/git/defra/trade-imports-workspace" (37 scripts, 134 files under tools/ and scripts/ name the canonical path) and have no override. tim resolves it per clone (tim/src/env/workspace-root.js:57-87). This is the config behind the fixed-path rule, and a port or a `--workspace`-style env (TIM_WORKSPACE) fixes it. scripts/stack/* are already relative to the script (run-stack.sh:5).

scripts/sonar/sonar-push-gate.sh:89 and scripts/sonar/sonar-check-pending.sh:18 hardcode the canonical path. sonar-check-pending.sh falls back to it only when CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR is unset, and tim has no equivalent of CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR. A port must take the root from the hook's cwd or CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, or a second clone's pushes go through the canonical clone's check script.

The `sonar` CLI's own stored login has no tim equivalent. scripts/sonar/sonar-check-pending.sh:39,44 calls `sonar api get /api/project_pull_requests/list` and `sonar list issues`, which use the SonarSource CLI's own auth store, not SONAR_TOKEN (not checked here which store it is). tim's sonar client covers issues and the gate verdict, but has no PR-list call and needs SONAR_TOKEN for private projects. Porting this script means users export SONAR_TOKEN, which the push gate already asks for.

JIRA_PROJECT_KEY is read differently by `tim jira create`. tools/jira/create-ticket.sh:184 and tools/jira/add-subtask.sh:182 require it from the env. `tim jira create` takes the project from its manifest (tim/src/commands/jira/manifest.js:18) and ignores the env. The manifest fills it in, so this is not a setup break, but a straight port of add-subtask should keep the env fallback, as epics.js:24 and search.js:54 do.

The Jira board id is written into the code in two places: tools/ticket-creator/prepare-ticket-creation.sh:19 and tim/src/commands/build/start.js:40, both 13780. Neither reads an env var. No `tim jira` command moves tickets to a board or lists board epics, labels or issues (tools/jira/move-to-board.sh, list-board-epics.sh, list-board-labels.sh, get-issues-for-board.sh); jira-client.js has moveToBoard but nothing else. These are command gaps, not credential gaps.

GitHub stays on gh by rule. tools/github/auth.sh:7 is part of tools/auth.sh. `tim auth` leaves GitHub out on purpose (tim/src/commands/auth.js:80), and rule 8 forbids wrapping gh in tim. tools/github/* and tools/github-actions/* should be retired in favour of plain `gh`, not ported. Users need no new token: gh keeps its own keychain or GH_TOKEN.

Stack knobs are passed through, not read natively. tim passes STUB_PROFILE, DEV_BUILD_PLATFORM, CI, NO_COLOR, MONGO_UP_ATTEMPTS, MONGO_RETRY_BACKOFF_SECONDS, TRADE_IMPORTS_*, ZAP_*, AUTH_PASSWORD, NUNJUCKS_* and the AWS/ASB endpoints only by running scripts/stack/*.sh with the environment inherited (tim/src/exec/exec.js). tim reads only STUB_PROFILE itself (stack-lease.js:38). A native port must keep each name and default from scripts/stack/lib/compose.sh:40-50, scripts/stack/lib/colour.sh:2-3, run-stack.sh:309-310 and the compose files, or users' overrides stop working without any warning.

The stack lease is one per machine (TIM_STACK_LEASE or ~/.local/state/tim/stack-lease.json, tim/src/exec/stack-lease.js:46-55), not one per clone. That suits several clones sharing one Docker stack. tim/src/build/machine-config.js:36 keeps config/machine.json per clone, though, so each extra clone has to rerun `tim build tune --write` or set TIM_MACHINE_CONFIG.
Local tool prerequisites go away. The Bash Jira and Confluence scripts need curl and jq on PATH (tools/jira/auth.sh:19-23); tim uses fetch. Nobody needs to change anything.

Unchecked: docker/stack/shared.env (the committed container env_file) could not be read because a secrets hook blocks it. It feeds the containers, not a user credential, and both Bash and tim reach it the same way through compose.

in-flight.overlapWithThisPlan:
HOW THIS BRANCH OVERLAPS THE PLAN

Phase 1 (move the bash into tim)
- This branch already does the first slice: Make into tim. The plan should start from this branch once it merges, not from main. Otherwise it repeats the start.js, docker logs and workspace-marker work and conflicts with them.
- It does not touch the bash that causes the hard-coded path. scripts/stack/*.sh already find their root from their own folder (run-stack.sh:5). The coupling is in:
  - 131 tools/*.sh with WORKSPACE="$HOME/git/defra/trade-imports-workspace"
  - .claude/settings.json:63-93 allowlist patterns
  - about 1,014 lines in .claude/skills/** that type the full path
  - tim/src/backlog/standards/rules.js:7 (WORKSPACE_PREFIX)
  - tim/src/constants/repos.js:21 and workspace-root.js:13-17 (fallbacks)
  - scripts/sonar/sonar-push-gate.sh:90
  - .claude/workflows/designer-prototyping-suite.js:45 (an absolute /Users/... path)
- So your guess is about two-thirds right. Moving tools/ into tim removes the script half. The allowlist and the paths written into skills are a separate fix, and it is the one that actually stops a second clone working.
- A cheap step before any port: replace the literal in tools/*.sh with a root found from the script's own location (as run-stack.sh does) or from CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR (as sonar-check-pending.sh:18 already does).
- Credentials need no change. tim already reads the same JIRA_USER, JIRA_TOKEN and JIRA_BASE_URL as the bash (tim/CLAUDE.md "Auth env vars").
- Two stale leftovers for the plan to tidy:
  - `tim link` help says "required by tools/" (link.js:112)
  - workspace-root.js's doc comment says "`tools/*.sh` hardcode this path"
- docker-local-branches was dropped with no replacement. Decide whether to port it or retire it on purpose.
- dockws/ is a leaked test fixture. It has nothing to do with this plan, apart from showing that some test once wrote a fixture relative to the current folder.

Phase 2 (several clones at once, one stack)
The machinery already favours one stack per machine, whichever clone started it:
- the compose project name is fixed: docker/stack/compose.yml:1 `name: trade-imports`, tim/src/exec/stack.js:86 STACK_PROJECT
- the lease file is per machine, outside every repo (tim/src/exec/stack-lease.js:44-58: TIM_STACK_LEASE or ~/.local/state/tim/stack-lease.json)
- so a second clone that tries to start the stack is refused instead of colliding

What still blocks parallel clones:
- Any clone not at the canonical path:
  - gets permission prompts, because the allowlist is tied to the path
  - has skills and tools that read and write the canonical clone's workareas/ and repos/ (e.g. tools/style/*.sh write workareas/code-style-reviews under $HOME/git/defra/...), so two clones silently share state
  - has a tim that falls back to the canonical clone when run outside its own tree
- The global `npm link` tim comes from one clone. tim then finds the workspace by walking up from the current folder, but the code that runs is that one clone's (see CLAUDE.md's `readlink -f "$(which tim)"` warning).
- The lease records holder, branches and stackFiles, but not the workspace root. A refusal cannot say which clone holds the stack.
- Each clone needs its own full repos/ (run tim workspace setup). Dev mode mounts ../../repos relative to the clone that started the stack, which is fine.

Conflicts with the older plan:
- workareas/shared/parallel-alt-stacks/plan.md wants several stacks on one machine, and its principle 5 is "scripts stay the single source of truth; tim is plumbing".
- This plan is the opposite on both counts: one stack, plus CI for end-to-end tests, and bash moved into tim.
- Treat the older plan as superseded, but reuse its audit. It lists which stack scripts parse flags (stop-stack.sh:20 forwards argv, restart-stack.sh calls stop with no args, bounce-mongo.sh claims $1), which this branch's --help work partly changes.

increments.risk: None in code: this is a documentation increment. The reasons to keep the hooks in Bash are real. (1) Self-protection: guard-edits.sh:37-41 protects only .claude/settings*.json and .claude/hooks/**. Moving the logic to tim/src/ would leave it editable by any agent, which defeats the guard against agents disarming their own guardrails (guard-edits.sh:2-13). Protecting tim/src/hooks too would block the build loop from maintaining the rest of tim. (2) Failing open: a Claude Code hook that exits non-zero with no deny JSON lets the command through. A tim hook on a fresh clone before `npm ci` in tim/, or with a stale tim/node_modules, would quietly turn every guard off. Bash plus jq has no install step. (3) Running against the wrong clone: `which tim` resolves through a global npm link to one clone (readlink shows ~/git/defra/trade-imports-workspace/tim/src/cli.js). With several clones, a `tim`-on-PATH hook would run another clone's guard code. Only a $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR-relative node call avoids that. (4) Cost: guard-bash runs before every Bash call, timeout 10s (settings.json:114). Node start-up plus commander loading on every call adds time, where a Bash script does not. (5) Neither hook calls a network service, Jira, Confluence or GitHub, so tim's library-first and nock rails gain nothing. Neither wraps gh, so rule 8's 'delete and call gh' does not apply. Multiple clones: neither hook stops a second clone working. Both resolve via $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, guard-edits matches on suffixes, and the uncommitted-executable check uses the git top-level of the file being run (guard-bash.sh:77). After the previous increment, nothing in this folder names the canonical path.

(2) The suite regex ^tests/[A-Za-z0-9._/-]+$ plus no '..' (normalise-suites.sh:21). A trailing '/' is added only when the last segment is non-empty and has no '.' (lines 25-28), and duplicates are dropped AFTER the slash is added (lines 29-33). (3) The tag regex ^@[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$, deduped in first-seen order, joined with '|' (normalise-tags.sh:17-25). increments.risk: Medium. This is the walker's and batch implementor's hottest path. Semantics to keep exactly: list --no-ui prints 11 TSV columns in the fixed order (review-items.sh:7-8,108-121). Nulls become empty cells. Filters are ANDed. A missing items file prints nothing and exits 0 (review-items.sh:86). JSON is a bare array with repo merged into each item. counts treats a null disposition as 'Pending' and groups by (disposition, status), with the printf layout '  %4d  %-15s  %s' and '—' for an empty status. With no files it prints {"breakdown":[],"total":0} (review-counts.sh:40-48). add stores line as a STRING (--arg, review-add-item.sh:78), unlike the per-file JSON. It creates {ticket,repo,items:[]} when the file is missing and prints the new id. mark derives status (Fix/Discuss→'Not Done'; Won't Fix/Auto-Resolved/Merged→'—'; ''→null). Merged needs a note matching ^merged into #N$. --note '' sets null, and a missing --note leaves notes alone (review-mark.sh:57-96). status only accepts ''|Not Done|Done|Failed|—. The confirmation lines 'Marked #N in R: Disposition=.., Status=..' and 'Updated #N ..' stay verbatim, since walkers read them. Skills that use --json now read `.result` from the envelope instead of a bare array; update every jq path in WALKER.md and BATCH_IMPLEMENTOR.md in the same increment.
increments.proof: R2 harness goldens for every filter combination, every disposition and status transition, the Merged note refusal, a missing item and a missing file, run against an anonymised copy of a real items.<repo>.json. Assert TSV stdout is byte-identical and `--json | jq .result` equals the bash JSON. Then run one walker session (`walk review <id>`) on a throwaway copy of a real review and diff items.json after the same keystrokes.

blockers.name: Compose project name `trade-imports`
blockers.claim: Not while only one clone runs the stack. This is the single-stack invariant the lease relies on: every clone addresses the same project. The hazard is that any clone can act on the stack another clone started. `docker compose up` from clone B with the same project name recreates clone A's containers from B's compose files and B's repos/. A `down` from B tears A's stack down (stop-stack.sh:42, `down --volumes --remove-orphans`). If the project name were made per-clone, tim's lease and port detection (stack.js:86/150, ports.js:54) would stop seeing the other clone's stack. So it must stay one machine-global name.
blockers.evidence: docker/stack/compose.yml:1 (`name: trade-imports`). No -p or COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME is set in scripts/stack/lib/compose.sh:6-15 or run-stack.sh:351. tim hardcodes the same name in tim/src/exec/stack.js:86 (STACK_PROJECT) and filters on it at stack.js:150. tim/src/build/ports.js:54 uses it too.

votes.reasoning:
The claim holds up. It is also not really a blocker: it argues the shared project name has to stay, and names a cross-clone hazard. The code shows that hazard is real, but only for a stack started by hand (no lease). A build-loop stack is already protected across clones.

1. **One project name per machine: confirmed.**
   - docker/stack/compose.yml:1 sets `name: trade-imports`.
   - scripts/stack/lib/compose.sh:6-15 only adds `-f` files. It sets no `-p` and no COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME.
   - run-stack.sh:351 (`docker compose ... up`) and stop-stack.sh:42 (`down --volumes --remove-orphans`) both use that project.
   - tim hardcodes the same name (tim/src/exec/stack.js:86), filters `docker ps` on it (stack.js:150) and compares against it in tim/src/build/ports.js:64. With a per-clone name, tim would stop seeing another clone's stack, so the name has to stay shared.

2. **A leased stack is already safe across clones.**
   - The lease file is one per machine, outside every checkout: `~/.local/state/tim/stack-lease.json` (tim/src/exec/stack-lease.js:44-58).
   - `tim docker up/dev/down/restart/bounce-backend` from any clone refuses while any lease exists (tim/src/commands/docker/index.js:52-55).
   - `acquireDecision` refuses `held` or `unleased` (stack-lease.js:140-145).
   - `releaseStack` refuses another holder's lease (stack-lease.js:481-490).

3. **A stack started by hand is not protected.** Once clone A runs `tim docker dev`, no lease exists, so index.js:52 lets clone B run:
   - `tim docker down`: stop-stack.sh:42 tears down A's containers and volumes, because compose matches on the project label alone.
   - `tim docker dev`/`up`: `docker compose up` recreates A's containers from B's files. The bind mounts are relative (dev.compose.yml:4,14 `../../repos/...`, database.compose.yml:22 `./.staged/...`), so they now point at B's checkout.

   Running scripts/stack/*.sh directly skips even the lease check.

   Nothing compares clones today. The lease records `workspace: workspaceRoot` (stack-lease.js:319), but nothing reads it back. The `unleased` refusal only guards a lease acquire, not `tim docker down` or `dev`.

So the shared name is the right invariant, and the hazard does happen when a stack is unleased.

votes.fix:
Keep `name: trade-imports`: it is what lets every clone, and the lease, see the one stack. Add a guard so one clone cannot act on a stack another clone started.

1. In tim/src/exec/stack.js, add `stackOwner()`. It reads the `com.docker.compose.project.config_files` label (or `working_dir`) from one running container in the `trade-imports` project. Compose sets those labels on every container itself, and they hold the starting clone's absolute docker/stack path.
2. In tim/src/commands/docker/index.js `makeStackAction`, after the lease check: if the stack is up and its owner is not `<this workspaceRoot>/docker/stack`, refuse the command unless `--force` is given. That covers up, dev, down, restart and bounce-backend. The message names the owning clone and says to take the stack down from there.
3. In tim/src/exec/stack-lease.js, make `acquireDecision` and `releaseStack` compare `lease.workspace` (already recorded at :319) with the caller's workspaceRoot, and refuse on a mismatch. Then a lease from clone A cannot be acquired or released from clone B under the same holder name.
4. Optional backstop for anyone running the scripts directly: run-stack.sh and stop-stack.sh do the same label check with `docker ps --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=trade-imports --format '{{.Label "com.docker.compose.project.working_dir"}}'` and refuse on a mismatch. Retiring direct script use in favour of tim, as the tim migration plans, closes this path as well.

votes.reasoning:
**Verdict: refuted as a blocker.** The evidence is accurate, but it describes the rule that makes "one clone owns the stack" work, not something that stops several clones. The real hazard is a small guard gap in `tim docker`, and it has a simple fix.

**The evidence checks out:**

| Claim | Where |
|---|---|
| The stack's project name is fixed | docker/stack/compose.yml:1 (`name: trade-imports`) |
| No `-p` or `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` is set | scripts/stack/lib/compose.sh:6-15 |
| Stop tears down the whole project, volumes included | scripts/stack/stop-stack.sh:42 (`down --volumes --remove-orphans`) |
| tim uses the same fixed name | tim/src/exec/stack.js:86 (`STACK_PROJECT`), filtered on at stack.js:150 |
| Port detection uses it too | tim/src/build/ports.js:64 (`workspaceStack: project === STACK_PROJECT`) |
| No container names are hardcoded | `container_name` count in docker/stack is 0, so only the project name keys the stack |

**Why it is not a blocker:**

- The lease is already per machine, not per clone: `TIM_STACK_LEASE` or `~/.local/state/tim/stack-lease.json` (tim/src/commands/docker/lease.js:233).
- Every clone reads the same lease file and the same project label. So the shared name is what lets clone B see that clone A's stack is up.
- Giving each clone its own project name would make things worse: clone B could start a second stack (the host ports would clash) and tim's lease and port checks would not see A's stack.
- So the fixed name must stay, and it suits the one-stack model the user described.

**The real gap (a small guard, not a design problem):**

- `tim docker up|dev|down|restart|bounce-backend` refuse only while a lease exists (tim/src/commands/docker/index.js:52-55).
- A stack started by hand with `tim docker dev`, with no lease, is not protected. From clone B, `up` would rebuild clone A's containers from B's compose files and `repos/`, and `down` would remove A's stack and its volumes.
- The lease records a holder and branches but not which clone started the stack (stack-lease.js:95-102), so tim cannot tell "my stack" from "another clone's stack".
- Running `scripts/stack/*.sh` directly skips every check. This is minor, since tim is meant to be the one entry point.

blockers.name: Lease-free stack commands: tim docker up/dev/down/restart/bounce-backend and the scripts called directly
blockers.claim: Yes. This is the real collision. Clone A runs `tim docker dev`, which takes no lease. Clone B then runs `tim docker dev` or `up`, which goes ahead and silently recreates A's containers from B's source. B's `tim docker down` wipes A's databases. bounce-backend.sh and `dev-service.sh rebuild` from B rebuild A's running backend from B's repos/. The same can happen today with one clone and a hand-started stack. It is more likely with several clones. Fix: make every stack-starting and stack-stopping command take or check the lease, and record and compare `workspace`.
blockers.evidence: tim/src/commands/docker/index.js:52-56 refuses only when a lease file exists. A stack started with plain `tim docker dev` writes no lease. The scripts themselves never read the lease: run-stack.sh, stop-stack.sh:42, bounce-backend.sh:46, dev-service.sh:58-71.

votes.reasoning:
The claim holds. I read the code and it shows the collision happens.

1. Plain stack commands check for a lease file and nothing else. In tim/src/commands/docker/index.js:52-56, makeStackAction reads the lease and refuses only when a lease file exists. It never writes a lease, and it never checks whether a stack is already running or which clone started it. up, dev, down, restart and bounce-backend all go through this path (index.js:122-151). So `tim docker dev` in clone A leaves no lease behind, and clone B's `tim docker dev`, `up` or `down` is not stopped.

2. Every clone drives the same Docker Compose project. docker/stack/compose.yml:1 fixes the project name as `name: trade-imports`, and the scripts take the workspace root from their own path (for example scripts/stack/dev-service.sh:16-18). The dev build contexts are relative to that root, `../../repos/<repo>` (docker/stack/dev.compose.yml:4-134), so each clone points them at its own repos/.

When B runs `docker compose up` against project `trade-imports`, Compose sees A's containers with a different configuration (different build context and bind-mount paths). It recreates them from B's source. Nothing warns anyone.

3. The scripts never read the lease. grep finds no lease check in run-stack.sh, restart-stack.sh, stop-stack.sh or bounce-backend.sh. The only mention is a comment in dev-service.sh:13. What each script runs:
- stop-stack.sh:42 runs `docker compose ... down --volumes --remove-orphans`, so B's `tim docker down` deletes A's database volumes.
- bounce-backend.sh:46 runs `up --force-recreate --no-deps` against the same project.
- `dev-service.sh rebuild` runs `up --build --no-deps` (lines 58-61) with B's build contexts.

4. The lease machinery could already guard this, but only the lease path uses it. The lease records `workspace: workspaceRoot` (tim/src/exec/stack-lease.js:319). `tim docker lease acquire` already refuses a stack that is running without a lease ("somebody started it by hand (tim docker dev, say)", stack-lease.js:153). The plain stack commands use none of this.

One part of the evidence is weak. dev-service.sh is documented as used by `tim build gate` while that gate holds the lease (dev-service.sh:12-13), so a person rarely runs it directly from clone B. It still has no guard of its own.

The gap also exists today with one clone and a stack started by hand. With several clones, that gap becomes routine, because every clone's commands land on the same project, `trade-imports`.

A side note from a read-only check: no lease file exists right now (~/.local/state/tim/ holds only logs/).

1. Before up, dev, restart or bounce-backend runs a script, makeStackAction in tim/src/commands/docker/index.js checks who owns the stack:

2. dev and up take a light ownership record when they start the stack. Either they write a lease with holder "manual", the mode and the workspace, or they rely on the working_dir label above. Either way, the next clone has something to compare against.

3. down refuses when the running stack's working_dir or lease workspace is a different clone, because `--volumes` deletes that clone's data. --force overrides.

4. Move the same check into the scripts as well, in a shared scripts/stack/lib helper that each script sources: compare the running containers' working_dir label with $STACK_DIR. Then running run-stack.sh, stop-stack.sh, bounce-backend.sh or dev-service.sh directly is guarded too. Once these scripts move into tim, the check lives in tim only.

blockers.name: Fit-test host ports 3050, 3052, 3053 (build-gate fit rungs)
blockers.claim: Only if two clones run the same frontend repo's fit suite at the same moment. The gate then refuses one with 'Port N is in use'. That is a refusal, not corruption. These rungs do not need the Docker stack, so clones with no stack would want them in parallel. Making them work in parallel would need port offsets.
blockers.evidence: .claude/skills/requirements-pipeline/references/gates.json:66-68, 117-119, 202-204. The gate refuses when a port is held: tim/src/build/gate.js:212-234 (heldPortReasons, runFitRung).

votes.reasoning:
The claim holds. I read the code and it does happen. The result is a clean refusal, not corruption.

1. The ports are fixed per frontend repo and nothing changes them per clone:
   - .claude/skills/requirements-pipeline/references/gates.json:66-68 sets plants-frontend to 3053.
   - gates.json:117-119 sets animals-frontend to 3050.
   - gates.json:202-204 sets ins-frontend to 3052.
   - Each repo's `test:fit:ci` script hard-codes the same number: repos/trade-imports-plants-frontend/package.json:24 (`PORT=3053`), repos/trade-imports-animals-frontend/package.json:23 (`PORT=3050`), repos/trade-imports-ins-frontend/package.json:25 (`PORT=3052`).
   - Two clones running the same repo's fit rung therefore ask for the same host port.

2. The gate checks the port before it runs:
   - tim/src/build/gate.js:230-234 (`runFitRung`) calls `heldPortReasons`. Any held port fails the rung with "Port N is in use by ... The rung needs it free." (gate.js:205-206) and stops it before `runRung`.
   - `isPortHeld` (tim/src/build/ports.js:28) probes both loopback addresses. So a second clone's rung fails while the first clone's fit server is up.

3. A race cannot cause corruption either:
   - Two clones could both pass the check before either server binds.
   - Every playwright.config.js sets `reuseExistingServer: false`: plants-frontend :74, animals-frontend :73, ins-frontend :46.
   - So Playwright errors when the port is taken and never attaches to the other clone's server. The worst case is a failed rung, not tests run against the wrong clone's code.

4. The rungs need no stack. The gate only consults the stack lease when the process holding the port is the workspace stack (gate.js:205-209, 217-224). Clones without a stack would reasonably want these rungs in parallel, and today they get a refusal.

Severity: the blocker is real but narrow. It only bites when two clones run the same frontend's fit suite at the same moment. Different frontends use different ports and do not clash.
votes.evidence:
- gates.json:66-68 sets 3053, :117-119 sets 3050, :202-204 sets 3052.
- The package.json `test:fit:ci` lines hard-code `PORT=3053` (plants-frontend:24), `PORT=3050` (animals-frontend:23) and `PORT=3052` (ins-frontend:25).
- tim/src/build/gate.js:212-234 checks the ports first (`heldPortReasons`) and fails the rung (`runFitRung`): `held.length > 0 ? failed(rung, held.join(' ')) : runRung(rung, context)`.
- tim/src/build/ports.js:28 is `isPortHeld`, which probes both loopback hosts.
- Each playwright.config.js sets `reuseExistingServer: false`: plants-frontend:74, animals-frontend:73, ins-frontend:46. A race therefore ends in a Playwright error, never in reuse of the other clone's server.

Give each clone its own fit port:

1. In each frontend's `test:fit:ci`, keep the number as the default only: `PORT=${PORT:-3053} npm run test:fit -- ...` (and the same for 3050 and 3052). Playwright already reads `process.env.PORT`.

2. In tim, give each clone a port offset, for example `TIM_PORT_OFFSET`, or one worked out from the clone's index or path. Add it to each fit rung's `ports` from gates.json. Pass the result as `PORT` in the rung's environment, so the check and the server always use the same port.

3. The canonical clone keeps offset 0, so its ports and existing setups do not change.

Without this, the refusal is safe. A clone just has to wait until the same frontend's fit suite finishes in the other clone.

blockers.name: Images built from local source by --dev (`trade-imports-trade-imports-<service>:latest`)
blockers.claim: Yes, but it is harmless with the lease rule. Clone B's dev build overwrites the tag clone A built. Each `-d` start passes --build, so whoever starts next rebuilds from their own repos/ (layer cache reused). The risk is a bare `up` or bounce after another clone's build: bounce-backend.sh:46 recreates without --build, and dev-service `restart` may then run the other clone's image. Fix: tag per clone, or always --build.
blockers.evidence: docker/stack/dev.compose.yml:9,27,44,55,66,77,... (`image: ''` with `build.context: ../../repos/<repo>`), so compose tags images `<project>-<service>:latest`. `docker images` shows trade-imports-trade-imports-animals-frontend:latest and the others. run-stack.sh:345 adds --build in dev mode. dev-service.sh:62 uses `up --build`.

votes.reasoning:
Two things in the claim hold up. The tag really is shared, and a -d start really does rebuild. Neither stops parallel clones.

1. The shared tag is real. docker/stack/compose.yml:1 fixes `name: trade-imports` whatever the clone's folder is called. Every dev service sets `image: ''` with a build context under ../../repos (docker/stack/dev.compose.yml:3-9, 22-27, 40-44, ...). So compose tags the images `trade-imports-trade-imports-<service>:latest`, and `docker images` lists 11 of them. Both clones write the same tag.

2. A -d start rebuilds every time. run-stack.sh:345 adds `--build` in dev mode. The owner's dev start always rebuilds from its own repos/, so the last clone to start the stack in dev mode is the one whose images the tags hold.

3. The claim about dev-service `restart` is wrong. dev-service.sh:66 runs `docker compose restart`, which keeps the existing container and its image. Line 69-70 then runs `up --no-deps --no-recreate`, which never recreates. A restart cannot pick up an image another clone built. Only `rebuild` (line 61-62, `up --build`) changes the image, and it rebuilds from its own source.

4. bounce-backend.sh:46 does recreate without `--build`, so it uses whatever the tag points at. That only goes wrong if the clone running the bounce does not own the running stack, which breaks the one-owner rule.
   - `tim docker bounce-backend` refuses while a build holds the lease (tim/src/commands/docker/index.js:52-54, 147-149).
   - The lease is one file per machine, shared by every clone (tim/src/exec/stack-lease.js:44-58).
   - Because the project name is fixed, a non-owner's bounce would take over the owner's backend container anyway: its compose files, its bind mounts of repos/.../src, its config. The image is the smallest part of that harm, and the fix is the ownership rule, not per-clone tags.

5. Within the lease rule the tags always match the owner's source. Only the owner runs `up --build` or `rebuild`. A new owner's dev start rebuilds everything before use. Build cache sharing is harmless: each layer is keyed on its content.

Verdict: not a blocker. The claim's own conclusion ("harmless with the lease rule") stands, but its restart scenario does not happen. The bounce scenario only happens when the ownership rule is broken.

votes.reasoning:
This blocker is real. A second clone writes into the first clone's files and branches.

The scripts do not look at where they are running. They look up the first clone's fixed path, so every read and write lands there. A second clone cannot avoid it, because the skills also type the first clone's full path when they call these scripts.

**Journey-builder digest.** `tools/journey-builder/prepare-digest.sh:16` sets the workspace to the fixed path. `tools/journey-builder/target-profile.sh:57` then points the frontend repo at `$WORKSPACE/repos/...` in the first clone. At :52-54 the script runs `git worktree add` in that frontend repo and creates a `spike/<run>-<suffix>` branch. At :75-77 it runs `git worktree add` on the first clone's own workspace repo and creates a `spec/<run>` branch from `main`. Both worktrees go under the first clone's `workareas/journey-builder/<run>/` (:38-42). So a digest run from the second clone creates branches and worktrees in the first clone's repos. That is the branch pollution the claim describes.

**Code-style tools.** `tools/style/style-add-item.sh:75` writes `items.<repo>.json` under the first clone's `workareas/code-style-reviews/`. `tools/style/aggregate-file-reviews.sh:49` reads that same folder. Two clones reviewing the same ticket and repo would write the same file.

So the second clone's own test edits are ignored.

**The skills call the first clone's copy.** `.claude/skills/service-tag/SKILL.md:57,108,146` and `.claude/skills/review/SKILL.md:291` call the scripts by their full fixed path. A session in the second clone therefore runs the first clone's copy of the script, against the first clone's data.

**How widespread.** 277 files under `tools/`, `scripts/`, `docker/`, `.claude/` and `tim/src` contain the path (the claim said about 268). `.claude/settings.json` has 18 lines that use it.

**One part of the claim is wrong.** These cross-clone writes are not the reason the path was fixed. They are a side effect of it. The original rule came in commit `eb8f0f44` (`docs/agent-onboarding.md` and `docs/agent-skills.md`, "Workspace root resolution"). It gives two reasons:
- **Running from anywhere:** a skill can start in any folder. From inside `repos/<service>`, `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` returns the service repo, not the workspace.
- **Permissions:** the `.claude/settings.json` allowlist patterns match a literal path.
